content_voiceover: This slide gives the updated survival data from the same PhALLCON trial, now looking at event free and progression free survival with longer follow up. Ponatinib enrolled one hundred sixty four patients and imatinib eighty one. For event free survival, censored for transplant, ponatinib had fewer events, twenty eight point seven percent versus thirty four point six percent with imatinib, and median event free survival was not even estimable in the ponatinib arm compared to twenty nine months with imatinib, though the hazard ratio of point six five had a confidence interval crossing one, so this difference didn't reach statistical significance. Progression free survival told a clearer story, ponatinib's median was twenty months versus just seven point nine months for imatinib, with a hazard ratio of point five eight and a tighter confidence interval of point four one to point eight three, which is statistically significant. Visually, both Kaplan-Meier curves separate early and the ponatinib line consistently sits above imatinib throughout follow up. The key nuance for boards is that while MRD negative CR and progression free survival clearly favor ponatinib, the event free survival benefit trended favorably but wasn't statistically definitive in this analysis, which is a common testable detail examiners like to probe.
keypoints: Ponatinib n=164 vs imatinib n=81, PhALLCON follow-up data
EFS: median not estimable vs 29 months, HR 0.65 (CI crosses 1)
PFS: median 20 months vs 7.9 months, HR 0.58 (significant)
PFS benefit is statistically robust; EFS trend not yet significant
keypoint_voiceover: Keep two numbers straight from this trial: progression free survival was clearly better with ponatinib, twenty months versus about eight months, and that result was statistically significant. Event free survival also favored ponatinib but its confidence interval crossed one, so it wasn't formally significant, a nuance worth remembering.
